meanings.note: Prefix 'с-' ('together' or 'down from') marks convergence or completion (stem 'казать'). Used as an perfective (single completed action) verb meaning 'say', paired with 'говорить'.

examples.text: Бабушка сказала, это не отец Кости.
examples.trans: Grandmother said this is not Kostya's father.
Thank you for not telling the police officers.

examples.text: Катюша, мне нужно кое-что тебе рассказать.
examples.trans: Katyusha, I need to tell you something.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'what, that', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: Obviously, this is a clever con artist.
Wait, did he pay the money after all?

examples.text: Он подтвердил, что он отец Кости.
examples.trans: He confirmed that he is Kostya's father.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian conversational adverb meaning 'here', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: Tell me, what is going on here?
Sit here completely quietly!

examples.text: Мама, а ты что тут делаешь?
examples.trans: Mom, what are you doing here?

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian spatial or relational preposition meaning 'for', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: Wait, did he pay the money after all?
Yes, he paid, of course.
Thank you for your answer.

meanings.note: Common neuter noun meaning 'things to do' in everyday Russian.

examples.text: Скажите, вы на самом деле инвалид?
examples.trans: Tell me, are you really disabled?
We need to do a paternity test.

examples.text: Я об этом в кино видела.
examples.trans: I saw about that in the movies.

meanings.note: Prefix 'с-' ('together' or 'down from') marks convergence or completion (stem 'мотреть'). Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'watch, look', paired with 'посмотреть'.

examples.text: Я хочу посмотреть, как вы готовите.
examples.trans: I want to watch how you cook.
Look what I've got.
I'm watching TV.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'you (informal)', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.text: Ты же сама его недавно нашла.
examples.trans: You found him recently yourself, after all.
Yes, I get tired, there is a lot of work.
Yes, you tried very hard.

meanings.note: Prefix 'с-' ('together' or 'down from') marks convergence or completion (stem 'овсем').

examples.trans: No, she is not against it at all.

examples.text: Я об этом совсем не знал.
examples.trans: I did not know about that at all.
I see you do not change at all.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian discourse particle adding conversational nuance meaning 'not', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.text: Без меня вы звезду не получите.
examples.trans: Without me you will never get a star.

examples.text: А Елена Павловна разве не против?
examples.trans: And is Elena Pavlovna not against it?
No, she is not against it at all.

meanings.note: Reflexive/intransitive verb with the postfix '-ся'/'-сь' (historically from the reflexive pronoun 'себя', oneself). Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'to change, alter', paired with 'поменяться'.

examples.trans: People change for the better.
Everything around is changing.

examples.text: Да, люди вокруг меняются к лучшему.
examples.trans: Yes, people around are changing for the better.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'this, it (is)', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: Chef, this is just an ordinary bolt.
Tell me, who cooked this?
Obviously, this is a clever con artist.

meanings.note: Common feminine noun meaning 'jokes' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: Misha, what kind of jokes are these?
Nastya, is this some kind of joke?
It's a joke.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian discourse particle adding conversational nuance meaning 'come on, well', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: Well, what kind of maniac is he?
For the test we need to take saliva.
And I read that hair is needed.

meanings.note: Agrees in gender, number, and case with the noun it modifies ('what').

examples.trans: Well, what kind of maniac is he?
Look how much the child loves him.
Believe me, I know what that is like.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'I', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.text: Без меня вы звезду не получите.
examples.trans: Without me you will never get a star.

examples.text: На два часа я её уговорил.
examples.trans: I talked her into two hours a day.
A guest found a piece of metal in the soup.

meanings.note: Common masculine noun meaning 'disabled person' in everyday Russian.

examples.text: Скажите, вы на самом деле инвалид?
examples.trans: Tell me, are you really disabled?
Well, how am I a disabled person to you?

examples.text: Инвалид пусть тихо сидит в кресле.
examples.trans: Let the disabled man sit quietly in his chair.

meanings.note: Negative prefix 'не-' ('un-, non-, not') (stem 'давно'). Manner/predicative adverb in '-о', derived from the neuter short form of the corresponding adjective.

examples.text: Ты же сама его недавно нашла.
examples.trans: You found him recently yourself, after all.
You recently came out of a coma.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian spatial or relational preposition meaning 'from/out of', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.text: Гость в супе из чечевицы нашёл.
examples.trans: The guest found it in the lentil soup.
This is a Michelin inspector from Paris!
His legs were completely paralyzed.

meanings.note: Common feminine noun meaning 'coma' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: Which one of us needs the star?
You recently came out of a coma.

examples.text: Патрик, познакомься, это моя жена Елена.
examples.trans: Patrick, meet my wife Elena.

meanings.note: Used as an perfective (single completed action) verb meaning 'stepped out, went out', paired with 'выходить'.

examples.text: Не мог выйти один на один?
examples.trans: Could you not face me one on one?

examples.text: Я выйду отсюда через две недели.
examples.trans: I'll be out of here in two weeks.
He left the house.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian conversational adverb meaning 'so', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: Wait, did he pay the money after all?
Unfortunately, such is our life.
So I did not even lie.

meanings.note: Prefix 'с-' ('together' or 'down from') marks convergence or completion (stem 'оврать'). Used as an perfective (single completed action) verb meaning 'lied', paired with 'врать'.

examples.trans: So I did not even lie.

examples.text: Потому что я соврал про деньги.
examples.trans: Because I lied about the money.
He never lied to his friends.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian discourse particle adding conversational nuance meaning 'only', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: Just do not get nervous right now.
I only embellished everything slightly.

examples.text: У меня её только что украли.
examples.trans: Someone just stole it from me.

meanings.note: Prefix 'с-' ('together' or 'down from') marks convergence or completion (stem 'легка').

examples.trans: I only embellished everything slightly.

examples.text: Костя сказал это совершенно слегка и спокойно.
examples.trans: Kostya said this quite slightly and calmly.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'everything', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: Wait, did he pay the money after all?
Little children sense everything right away.
Am I telling everything correctly?

meanings.note: Prefix 'при-' indicates approaching, attachment, or slight degree of action (stem 'украсить'). Used as an perfective (single completed action) verb meaning 'embellished'.

examples.trans: I only embellished everything slightly.

examples.text: Надо всё сделать и приукрасить вовремя.
examples.trans: We need to do everything and embellished on time.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'to him', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: No, she is not against it at all.
Now he wants to see the chef.
They simply do not want to pay!

meanings.note: Prefix 'про-' indicates movement through, completion, or missing the mark (stem 'стой'). Agrees in gender, number, and case with the noun it modifies ('simple').

examples.trans: They simply do not want to pay!
That is simply a great idea, Dad!
You are simply a true hero, Viktor!

meanings.note: Common masculine noun meaning 'cheburek (fried turnover)' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: Fry him a simple cheburek.

examples.text: На кухне отеля всегда есть чебурек.
examples.trans: In the hotel kitchen there is always cheburek.

meanings.note: Prefix 'по-' forms perfective verbs or marks a brief/onset action (stem 'жарить'). Used as an perfective (single completed action) verb meaning 'fry'.

examples.text: Надо всё сделать и пожарить вовремя.
examples.trans: We need to do everything and fry on time.

examples.text: На нашей кухне все умеют пожарить.
examples.trans: In our kitchen everyone knows how to fry.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian clause-linking conjunction meaning 'and', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.text: Без меня вы звезду не получите.
examples.trans: Without me you will never get a star.

examples.text: А Елена Павловна разве не против?
examples.trans: And is Elena Pavlovna not against it?
No, she is not against it at all.

meanings.note: Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'will be'.

examples.trans: I just want to stay at home.
I have a toy car.
Childhood was hard.

meanings.note: Adjective formed with the common Slavic suffix '-н-' from a noun/verb root. Agrees in gender, number, and case with the noun it modifies ('culinary').

examples.trans: And it will be a culinary masterpiece!
After all, he is a true culinary fanatic.
He showed excellent culinary skills.

meanings.note: Common masculine noun meaning 'masterpiece' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: And it will be a culinary masterpiece!
A masterpiece was made out of nothing.
This soup is a real masterpiece.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian clause-linking conjunction meaning 'and, but', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.text: А Елена Павловна разве не против?
examples.trans: And is Elena Pavlovna not against it?
No, she is not against it at all.

examples.text: На два часа я её уговорил.
examples.trans: I talked her into two hours a day.

meanings.note: Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'know'.

examples.text: Я об этом совсем не знал.
examples.trans: I did not know about that at all.
That means this man is a sly swindler!
Believe me, I know what that is like.

meanings.note: Prefix 'по-' forms perfective verbs or marks a brief/onset action (stem 'чему').

examples.trans: Why is this happening to me?
And do you know why it will be like that?

examples.text: Почему я опять должен вам верить?
examples.trans: Why should I believe you again?

meanings.note: Prefix 'с-' ('together' or 'down from') marks convergence or completion (stem 'ейчас').

examples.trans: Right now I will go sort it out myself.
Just do not get nervous right now.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'our', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: A guest found a piece of metal in the soup.

examples.text: Гость в супе из чечевицы нашёл.
examples.trans: The guest found it in the lentil soup.

meanings.note: Adjective formed with the common Slavic suffix '-н-' from a noun/verb root. Agrees in gender, number, and case with the noun it modifies ('main').

examples.trans: He is their very chief inspector.

meanings.note: Common masculine noun meaning 'ingredient' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: Right now you are our main ingredient.

examples.trans: Chef, this is just an ordinary bolt.

meanings.note: Common feminine noun meaning 'idea / venture' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: They definitely need to take blood there.

meanings.note: Reflexive/intransitive verb with the postfix '-ся'/'-сь' (historically from the reflexive pronoun 'себя', oneself). Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'pleases', paired with 'понравиться'.

examples.trans: I like coffee.
